utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic, you are continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Before I continue my examination-in-chief, I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that immediately before the beginning of the session, in a conversation with Mr. Zaric, I was informed that Mr. Zaric has checked and that the therapy that he was supposed to receive has not been discontinued. I'm saying that because the Trial Chamber was misinformed yesterday about the therapy having been discontinued. Mr. Zaric did not get his therapy for reasons unknown to us, and that's why he suffered increased pain during his walk earlier this morning. Today he took his medicine again, and he is now ready to continue with his testimony. We were of the opinion that the Trial Chamber should be aware of this because Mr. Zaric is indeed ill but determined to finish his testimony before this Trial Chamber in order to provide for the efficiency of these proceedings. So much about that and so much about my conversation with Mr. Zaric upon the approval of the Trial Chamber. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We are grateful that you have given us the correct information. We would like to emphasise that the Trial Chamber, if at any time he feels like discontinuing, then he should let us know and we can discontinue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zaric, yesterday we talked about the 4th Detachment, and now I would like to move on to another topic. My question to you is whether you ever heard of a proclamation of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac. This is Exhibit P79. I don't insist on showing it to Mr. Zaric because Mr. Zaric, I'm sure you will remember that.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember it, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember when this was published and how?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, but it was aired on the radio on several occasions. I think that I heard it in the radio when I was driving with Mr. Toso Tutnjevic. I believe that this was on the 19th of April, 1992. But whether it was published even before that, I don't know. I heard it on a Sunday. But this is something that was repeated on Radio Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You said you heard it in the car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. I know -- we all know the exhibit numbers and so on, but to make sense of this question and answer maybe it would be good to give what the title of that proclamation was, rather than talk about whether Mr. Zaric heard it and so on and so forth, just to make sense for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Number P79.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I would kindly ask the usher to put Exhibit P79 before Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, look at the document and tell us whether the contents of this document, of this proclamation, is the same that you heard while driving in the car.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the same proclamation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how did you hear this in the car?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. This still isn't answering my question, which is for the sake of clarity, could we please -- I wasn't asking for Mr. Zaric to see the document. You said that wasn't necessary. I simply asked what was the proclamation about, for the sake of the clarity of the record and for the sake of clarity between your questions and Mr. Zaric's answers. So could we just have the title of the proclamation, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, please, could you tell us what you see in the upper left corner of this document.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I can't see too well, despite the fact that I am wearing my glasses. I can't read the first part, where it says "Municipality," and the next few words are illegible. But later on I can see that it says "and Pelagicevo municipality under foundation." Beneath that it says, "Crisis Staff, number 01-10-92. Date, 17 April 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read the title as well?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the middle of this document there is a big title, "Proclamation."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And at the end of the document, what can you see?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of the document, there is a -- there are the following words: "The Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac," and there are also two seals, two stamps. Rather illegible. I can't identify these two stamps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Perhaps if Your Honours please, P79 might be perhaps more succinctly identified in the transcript if we refer to it as announcement of the establishment of the Serbian Crisis Staff and the seizure of power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. That -- that clarifies it, Mr. Di Fazio. Thank you. That's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the document speaks for itself. We are not going to go into its contents. All I wish to know is whether this is the same thing you heard in your car.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the announcement that I heard in the car, and I heard it in the following way: In the car that was driven by Mr. Toso Tutnjevic there was a radio cassette player and this could receive amongst other things Radio Samac because that was the frequency that it could receive, the frequency of Radio Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was that announcement aired on Radio Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was aired on Radio Samac, and a female speaker read this announcement at the moment when I heard it in the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will no longer need this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, were you ever in a situation to hear on the Radio Bosanski Samac Mr. Sulejman Tihic addressing the general public?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear Mr. Sulejman Tihic on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sulejman Tihic appeared on the radio about the same time when I heard this announcement, on the 19th of April, 1992. I was not in the car all the time but I heard from my driver that this announcement had been repeated several times, so Sulejman Tihic's story that he heard and that I originally heard on the 19th was also repeated before that and I had the occasion to hear it on the 19th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember who Mr. Tihic addressed when he appeared on the radio?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic had a brief conversation. It was more of an announcement. He addressed the citizens of Bosanski Samac, but I believe that he -- his target audience were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what Mr. Tihic said in that address?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Mr. Tihic appealed to people, asking them to hand over all the armaments to the legal organs of the municipality and he said that the Serbian government had been introduced in the territory of Samac and that he had been promised that while after the arms were handed over new democratic order would be established, that the situation would become normal, and he asked people to accept that as a fact. This is how I would paraphrase his speech. In any case, this was the way I understood that address of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zaric. The 4th Detachment, did it also draft some sort of an announcement?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to put Exhibit D28/4 before Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, before you is D28/4. This is the announcement by the 4th Detachment. Is that the document that you were referring to as the document drafted by the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is precisely that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who drafted the announcement?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I and Mr. Rajko Iliskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: This document, this announcement, was it adopted by the command of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And as far as I can remember, this announcement as early as on the 17th in the evening hours, it was drafted on the 18th. It was typed out. It was checked against the instructions of our command as to the way we should address our citizens at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where did you take this announcement and who took it there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Rajko Iliskovic, who is -- who was a member of the 4th Detachment and also a person who is a gifted writer, and the two of us were the authors of this text, so he went on the 18th in the afternoon and took this announcement to the Radio Samac and gave it to Mr. Antic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you know whether this radio was ever aired on Radio Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear it being read?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it being read on the radio on the 19th of April, not at the same time as the announcements that I mentioned a little while ago. Mr. Rajko Iliskovic told me that on the 18th of April in the evening he had read this text to Mr. Antic, and I was told that Rajko himself read this text once on Radio Samac. On the 19th, when this text was read, it was read by a lady speaker who was an employee of Radio Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We don't seem to have any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't need this document any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It seems that we are receiving the English translation on the B/C/S channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I just heard English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have adjusted the channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is it all right now? I hear that they have adjusted the channels. Yes, we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, what happened after the announcement of the 4th Detachment was broadcast over the radio, over Radio Samac? What happened to you personally?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a very unpleasant incident on the premises of the public security station because of this announcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who summoned you to the police station, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was summoned there by Mr. Milos Culapovic, who was wearing a police uniform. He came to the command of the 4th Detachment, which was then in the area we call Sljivik or more precisely in Jovo Dusanovic's house, and this part of town is in the west part of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did Mr. Culapovic tell you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Culapovic said that I was being urgently summoned to report to the public security station, that Mr. Todorovic was asking for me, and so were the specials from Serbia. Mr. Culapovic's summons took place at around 11.00 a.m., as far as I can remember. This was the time when I was summoned to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you go there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived, who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was brought to the public security station by my driver, Toso Tutnjevic. And when I reported to the duty officer, Dimitrije Djordjic, telling him that the chief and some other people wanted me, he told me I should go upstairs straight to the office which said "Commander of police station" on the door. That's what it said on the entrance to that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to that office, and who did you find there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's one detail I'd like to mention. As I was going down the corridor, in the courtyard of the SUP, which was on the northern side, in the direction of the River Sava, about 50 or 60 young men were lined up in the courtyard. They all had painted faces. They were all wearing camouflage uniforms. Some of them had hats on; some had red berets, and some Balaclava helmets. You could see only the eyes. And I saw these lads there as I was going upstairs to the office where I had been told to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And who did you find there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I entered the office, I found three men I didn't know there. One of them was sitting at his ease. His coat was flung over his shoulders because he had a big bandage on this side. He had been wounded. I can't be sure as to whether it was his left or his right side, but he was leaning back at his ease in the armchair and his coat was just thrown over his shoulders and his hand was in a sling. He was holding his hand like this. That's how I saw him sitting in the armchair. The other two - whose names I would learn later - one of them was called Crni, that's Dragan Djordjevic, also known as Crni. And the third man who had a red beret on his head was called Aleksandar Vukovic, also known as Vuk. But except per his nickname Vuk, I didn't know anything else about him at the time. All I knew was his nickname, Vuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone please for counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Your microphone, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, when you entered the office and saw these men there, did you know who they were or what their names were?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't know who they were, nor did I know their names. And when I came in, I was wearing an old olive-grey uniform of the JNA, and on my head, as it so happened at that moment, was the so-called Tito cap, but without a five-pointed star, as the real insignia, so it wasn't the badge-type five-pointed star made of metal, but instead at the front of the cap there was a five-pointed star that had been sort of painted on, and this was the symbol of the army during the time of Tito. That was the uniform I was wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You have described it for us now. Tell us what happened when you entered the office. Did you address them? Did they address you? Who spoke first?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came in and said good day. Crni, who speaks very fast, immediately said Tito's greeting. When I said, "Good day," he said that I had greeted him in the way Tito's people do. I was a little taken aback by this. The young man said, "Oh, so you are that Zaric." I said, "Gentlemen, I am Simo Zaric, deputy commander of the 4th Detachment for security, and I would like to know was it you who summoned me. I'd like to know who you are and what you want." I was very sober in my actions. I didn't know these people, so I answered them in a manly way, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, this man Debeli, who had his coat on, said, "Mr. Zaric, sit down at this chair." He spoke in a commanding tone of voice. I sat down, and then a discussion started. They were vying with each other, Crni and Debeli.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What were they discussing?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said to me, "Mr. Zaric, what sort of communist pamphlets are you broadcasting over the radio?" I said, "Gentlemen, I'm not writing any sort of Communist pamphlets. This is an announcement by the command of the detachment and we published it." "We know all about you. You are at the head of the movement for Yugoslavia. You are at the head of the League of Communists, the movement for Yugoslavia. And it's those kind of people who have brought us to this pass." I said, "You can't talk to me like that. I don't want to talk to you in this way." And the young man said, "Did your balinkura tell you these things?" When he used the word "balinkura," I knew they meant my esteemed wife Fatima, who is an ethnic Muslim, and I saw that things were bad. Then I said, "I am not one of the leaders of the movement for Yugoslavia, nor is my wife a balinkura. My wife is a Muslim. And if you can speak in a decent tone, all right. But if not, I'm going." Then the young man with the red beret on came up behind me, behind the chair where I was sitting, and he grabbed me by the hair suddenly, pulled my head up, pulled out his pistol - that was a Roda pistol. That's the type of pistol. That's the brand - and this pistol was used during World War II. It was a kind of trophy weapon. It was quite rare. And this pistol had an especially long barrel. And he said, "Open your mouth," and he thrust the barrel into my mouth towards the left side. He pushed it down my throat and he said, "I fuck your Communist mother. Talk." At that moment I thought I would be dead within a few seconds. And if the Chamber will believe me, I didn't regret dying, but I thought, what has happened to Simo Zaric? Up to this moment I had the feeling that I was somebody in this town, and now all of a sudden I was facing some people who pretended to be patriots, who said they were here to defend Serbs, and yet they were thrusting a pistol barrel down my throat. This man Debeli then said, "Vuk, leave the man alone. Let it go." He pulled the pistol out of my mouth. I pulled myself together. I'm ashamed to say this, but I had to spit out some blood because he had hurt the roof of my mouth. Then Crni said to me, "Listen, brother Zaric [as interpreted]," I have to say this quite vividly because he speaks in the Vranje dialect and he speaks very fast. So it's very hard to understand what he's saying, even though he's an ethnic Serb. But the people who live in that part of Serbia, they speak so fast that they alone can understand each other and communicate with each other. He said, "Forget what happened here." And then the situation calmed down and Mr. Debeli said to me calmly, "Zaric, we are here as your brothers. We are here to help you. We have come here representing the Radicals and we are not interested in any sort of politics. The fact that you're at the head of some sort of League of Communists of Yugoslavia, forget about this. This no longer exists. We all have to be united now." That's what this man said to me very calmly. That was the man with his arm in a sling, and his nickname was Debeli. He said, "I am Debeli. This is Crni, and this is Vuk." So when they introduced themselves, it was always by nickname. I didn't know their real names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, what did this Debeli mean when he said "We all have to be the same"? What did he mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wanted to let me know that neither I nor the 4th Detachment could implement any sort of policy of our own. They were there to defend some kind of Serbdom. I don't know what kind of Serbdom, because this cost us dearly, the Serbdom they were there to protect. And when he said that he was there on behalf of the Radicals, he was a deputy in Serbia, a deputy of the Radical Party. And thanks to his merits, in Samac Seselj promoted him to the rank of vojvoda [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: But I still have not got a reply from you. What did he mean when he said, "We all have to be united, we all have to be together"?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... well, here we have two things. One is on page 12, line 11. Here it says, "Listen brother Zaric." Mr. Zaric, when he was referring to what -- to what this Debeli guy said to Mr. Zaric -- I apologise Crni said to Mr. Zaric, he used the word "Bre" and this doesn't mean "brother." So he never said to Mr. Zaric that he is some sort of brother to him. And the other thing is on page 13, line 9, I believe the meaning of this sentence has changed, because here after -- here it says, "And thanks to his merits -- thanks to his merits in Samac, Seselj promoted him to the rank of vojvoda" and this might actually mean that it happened actually in Samac that Seselj was in Samac where he promoted this guy as duke, the way it is written here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure Mr. Pisarevic will ask Mr. Zaric to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did Crni ever call you brother when he addressed you, or did he use the word "Bre", "Listen Bre Zaric"?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He used the word "Listen Bre Zaric," not "Brother Zaric." "Bre" is a word which is often used in the Serbian dialect where Serbs live in Serbia, in Yugoslavia, and it's not usual among Serbs living in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And tell us, please, where did Mr. Vojislav Seselj, if you know, promote Mr. Debeli to the rank of duke or vojvoda? Where was this?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We read about this later in the papers. It was published in the newspapers. There was a list of people whom Seselj had promoted to the rank of vojvoda. This could have been in 1993 or 1994. I read a newspaper saying that Srecko Radovanovic, Debeli, had been promoted to the rank of vojvoda, or duke.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember where this promotion took place? Was it on a mountain, in a town? Where was this?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where this was. It was somewhere in Serbia. But in the media I read about this. I couldn't tell you now where this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did it happen in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. As far as I know, Mr. Seselj never came to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, though. Mr. Zaric, based on what we saw -- this was based on merits, presumably of what he had done. Was it based on the merits according to the person who promoted him a duke? Was it based on the merits of what he had done in Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is my opinion. I said that this was my opinion. When other dukes were promoted, amongst those names in the newspaper we also read the name of this Srecko Radovanovic, Debeli. So I drew the conclusion that this was because of his merits while he was participating in the war in the area of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And do we interpret "merits" to mean actions, what he did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, Mr. Seselj always spoke very -- very well about all of the people that he sent to fight and because Mr. Srecko Radovanovic was at the head of such a unit, I don't know which criteria they applied in order to promote someone into a duke, and I don't know whether Mr. Seselj also had in mind all the negative things that had taken place and that are linked to all of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, Her Honour Judge Williams was interested in the following: When you said "merit," did you imply with that term the activities undertaken by Mr. Srecko Radovanovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I am thinking of, because of all that he did during the war, activities in the area of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And how did this meeting end?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting ended in the following way: "You may go. Be wise so that we do not have to meet again regarding these matters." I left the office. And believe me, I was completely broken. This Vuk came out behind me, the one with the red beret. And at the point just as I was about to go down the stairs and go towards my car, where Toso, the driver, was waiting for me, he said, "Just one moment, Mr. Zaric. Could you please just go into the SUP yard." And he took my sleeve, and instead of going to the right towards the exit, he turned me to the left. And I came out before this unit that was lined up, and I saw it as I was going up the stairs before. But he went up to this young man who was standing in front of these people from the unit and he said something to him, and then this young man turned to me and said - and that was actually Mr. Lugar - and he said, "Brothers, we have come here to bleed, but as far as our brother Serbs here are concerned we have this Tito's partisan here from the people who are here." And I stood there petrified. And then he continued, "While we're getting killed and dying out here, he's defending the Turks and the Ustashas." I was completely at a loss. I couldn't recognise any of the people who were there. There were about 50 or 60 men lined up in two columns. They were completely equipped with military equipment. They had hand grenades hanging from their belts. They were fully equipped. They looked quite terrifying. Some swore at my traitor mother, some cursed my balija mother, and I was afraid that somebody would just take their weapon and that it would be all over for Simo Zaric. But what was a handicap and what was shameful for me is the following: To the right of the entrance, Mr. Stevan Todorovic was standing like this, next to the wall. His hands were behind his back. He was wearing some kind of special black uniform, a police uniform, which was rarely or practically never seen in our area. He was also wearing a black beret, not a navy or blue beret but some kind of black special beret, and there were a few of our police officers who were peeking out through the windows, but none of them dared say a word. When Lugar said this, "We are going to our jobs now and we will deal with this trash when we want to," then that was one of the most difficult moments for me during the war, even though I did have some difficult moments later on. But this was my beginning in this war, as it began in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, were you afraid for your life? Were you afraid for the safety of your family?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not so brave to be able to just survive all of that, just simply like that. I was just thinking at that point that I was just happy that my family was not there at that point. I wasn't worried about myself when they put the barrel of the pistol in my mouth. This was the only thing that I was thinking about that, this war wouldn't last too long [as interpreted]. But really, I was very afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We have some problems of translation. Here it says on page 17, line 14, "This war wouldn't last too long." Literally Mr. Zaric said that, "I was not afraid of that. It is just one shot, and that doesn't last long." This is literally what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We shall accept that then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And where did you go after that and who did you go with?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got into the car with Mr. Toso, and I told him to take me to the command of the 4th Detachment, and I just managed to tell him, "Toso, I almost got killed in there." That was the only sentence that I had the strength to utter, to tell him what happened. I said to him, "I will tell you when we get to the command. I can't wait to get there so that I can have a little bit of water and collect myself."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did you get to the command?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I arrived at the command, and this could have been perhaps at about 1.00 p.m. or a little bit after 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And who was there at the command when you got there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Antic was there, as well as Deputy Jovo Savic, also Vlado Sisic was there, one of our commanders, one of our company commanders was there, one of the communications officers. His name was Bojic, Stanko Bojic, he was a communications officer, and a couple of other people who happened to be at the command at that time. Because when I -- when I left, when Culap called me, I told Commander Antic that they were calling me to go and that I would come back quickly, and that is how I came back also.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did you tell them what happened to you at the police station?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I told them everything. As much as I had the strength to tell them, I told them what happened to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Zaric, did you take any other steps to inform anybody else about what you had been through?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I asked the commander that I wanted to inform the commander of the 17th -- the command of the 17th Tactical Group about what had happened and I wanted him, if he was able to go with me, to see Commander Nikolic, that he and I go together to see him, and also to go and see Makso Simeunovic. We called them there, over the radio, and we received the information that at that point Commander Nikolic was not there but that he would be there in the afternoon and that it wasn't a problem for Commander Antic and myself to drop by. My entire story, which I relayed to Mr. Maksimovic, was that I had experienced a terrible problem and that I wanted him to hear from me about that personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Before you went to the commander of the 17 Tactical Group, did you inform anyone else about what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a little later, when I had collected myself somewhat, I decided to go to the agricultural cooperative where the Crisis Staff was and to try --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who did you meet at the Crisis Staff, at the agricultural cooperative?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the people who I remember being there, I saw Mr. Blagoje; Mr. Milan Simic; Stevan Todorovic was already there; Bozo Ninkovic was there; Mitar Mitrovic was there. I -- perhaps Savo Popovic was there also, Mr. Milos Bogdanovic was there. So they were all there in two offices. So these are the people that I found there, and this was in one of the administrative buildings of the agricultural combine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And who did you go to see there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the office of the president of the Crisis Staff, went to see Mr. Blagoje, and Milan Simic happened to be there with him at that point, as well as Stevo, and I also think that Mr. Milos Bogdanovic was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did you talk about with Mr. Simic and the others on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told them briefly what happened to me and I told them that Mr. Stevo watched this scene in the yard and I said, "I don't know what this can lead to. Is this supposed to be some kind of intra-Serb war?" I wasn't even sure whether the 4th Detachment and the people would back me at that point, but I tried to instill courage for myself and I said that if anybody wanted any kind of conflict like that, I need to take certain steps concerning the 4th Detachment, and then what would happen would happen. So that was the gist of my reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And how did Mr. Blagoje Simic and the others react to the way that you reacted to what had happened to you? I'm thinking of the others who attended this conversation.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say very truthfully that Mr. Blagoje was a little bit surprised with what I had told him. The only thing he said was that the military should not interfere in politics. And when he said that, I felt that the comment of Mr. Simic regarding this announcement was finished regarding this matter. But then there was a whole tirade [Realtime transcript omitted the word "tirade"] by Mr. Todorovic regarding this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Todorovic tell you [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milan Simic and Mr. Todorovic vied about who would insult me more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, maybe Mr. Zaric could possibly speak a little bit slower just for the transcript. I understand that he's very upset with this topic. First of all, we have here on page 20, Mr. Zaric said, "There was a whole --" he used the expression cannonade from Milan Simic and Stevan Todorovic regarding this. So he mentioned Mr. Milan Simic. And then Mr. Pisarevic asked, "And what did Mr. Todorovic and Mr. Milan Simic tell you?" That is the correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did Mr. Todorovic tell you, first, what did he tell you first? And then you will tell us what Mr. Simic told you.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Todorovic told me, "It doesn't surprise me if you're going around pretending to be some kind of a Commie and you're defending the Turks." At that point he would use the term "Turks" to refer to Muslims. "You are pulling them out of jail, while our brothers, Serbs, are dying here on the front." While, Milan Simic, who surprised me greatly - and later I understood that Milan is actually a person that I did not actually know all that well - in that context he told me, "Enough of politics and people like you, because I have a frustrated person like you at home, a person like you." And then when he said that he had a person like me at home, he actually meant his father, Vojo, because later and during the testimony this will also come up, he mentioned that before to me. Mr. Blagoje Simic tried to calm the situation down. He told both of the men to calm down; also, he told me to calm down. We spoke with raised voices, and I must say that I was quite angry and I said that I would inform my commander about what had happened to me and that this was simply something that I would not bear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did you manage to get to the commander of the 17 Tactical Group, Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And when I left, Milan Simic told me, "Tell the commander to teach you not to be involved in politics but to only involve yourself with the military." That was his message when I left the office. In the afternoon, Mr. Antic and myself, together with Toso Tutnjevic, went to the command of the 17th Tactical Group, and I informed Commander Nikolic and the security officer, Mr. Makso Simeunovic, in detail about all that had happened to me in Samac that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did Commander Nikolic tell you? What steps would he take? What did he say?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he would do everything that, he would warn them that they could not behave like that towards the military. He also did in fact say that it would have been a good thing for this announcement, which we released internally as a command, had he also been a little bit more informed about this announcement. Antic and myself then said that in order to effect a better homogenisation of the 4th Detachment and to -- and because of the overall atmosphere in the town itself, because we had seen all kinds of events and heard all kind of stories, it was our wish to encourage the people to join the 4th Detachment because we believed it to be a unit which had the proper attitude towards all of the people, regardless of their ethnicity. And that is why we were guided by the desire to propagate in a positive way the position of the 4th Detachment and its status, because we thought that we would get more points in that way and that some people then would believe that the 4th Detachment enjoyed somewhat more authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to ask the witness to slow down a bit. And then, on page 22, line 13, it reads, "He said that he would do everything that, he would warn them," and you find the same word also later on. What do you mean by "them"? Could you be a bit more precise in that sense.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic meant the representatives of the authorities. And in more specific terms, Mr. Todorovic, who at that moment showed the most impertinent attitude towards me, and he also meant those specials. He said that he would try to talk to them and tell them that they were not supposed to behave like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Commander Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic indeed talk to any of the representatives of the authorities with Todorovic and the leaders of the specials?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that because one part of the conversation took place while Antic and I were there, and another conversation that I remember very well was a conversation that he had with Mr. Blagoje. He told him in that conversation that this was not a good thing to have happened. And then after the conversation with Mr. Simic he immediately proceeded to talk to Mr. Todorovic, and already that conversation between Mr. Todorovic and Commander Nikolic ended up on a very sour note, that there was a lot of convincing going on, and Blagoje told him that certainly this was not a good thing that happened to Simo, but Blagoje also told the commander that the army should stay out of the politics, to which Nikolic replied that he knew exactly what kind of an announcement we broadcast and that from now on the army would engage in its own business. And he also informed Mr. Stevan Todorovic that from then on he would not allow any member of the JNA to be mistreated in such a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, after these events, were you afraid for your family?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. That is something that was always on my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you do about that? How did you protect your family?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For two days I kept quiet and I did not tell them immediately what had happened to me. I wanted to keep that a secret from them. However, after the conversation that I had on the 20th of April, 1992 in the public security station with Mr. Tihic, and when again I witnessed certain scenes and certain relationships there, finally I realised that I should protect my family. And one or two days later I asked a friend of mine whether there was any possibility for him to bring my family out to the safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is it now the time for our break, or should I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, before the break I asked you what you did to protect your family. So please tell us, how did you protect your family?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 21st of April, 1992, I moved my family, my wife, Fatima, and my sons, Denis and Mirel out of Bosanski Samac. In the evening hours of that day, I sent them away to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How did you send them to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that, I got in touch with a friend of mine whose name is Mico Vidovic. He was a driver in the company that I was the director of, and he drove a lorry that transported furniture. When I confided in him and asked him to help me take my family out of Samac, he told me that on the 21st of April he was to take his lorry towards Serbia and that there were some other families who were scheduled to go with him. He told me that it would not be a problem for him to take my family as well. The only suggestion he had for them was not to take a lot of personal belongings. That's exactly what happened. In the evening, he drove my [as interpreted] car to -- in front of my entrance, the entrance number 4 in the building where I resided. I didn't want my neighbours to see that my family was leaving. I had my own opinion about families leaving. If one's family is sent away, then this instills fear among neighbours. However, bearing in mind everything that had been through, that's what I decided. I put them in his car, and he gave them a lift to Srpska Tisina. That's where the lorry was. And the other passengers gathered there. And on that same evening they went via Brcko and Bijeljina and they arrived in Belgrade around midnight on the 22nd of April. They arrived in the area called Bezanija.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one small correction. In the transcript, page 25, line -- line 14 -- 15, sorry, "In the evening he drove his car," not "my car." That's the only thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, that's the correction. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you've used the term "closed lorry." Can you describe that lorry? You said that it was closed.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a cargo vehicle ranging in length between 8 and 12 metres. There are some smaller roll lorries. There are some bigger lorries. These are special purpose lorries for the transport of furniture and similar type of cargo. Once you close the door on that lorry, it becomes a problem for the passengers because there's no air in the lorry. That's why he had to make sure that the passengers had air. He made some openings in the canvas cover of that lorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you keep it a secret from others that your family had left? And if so, why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I kept it a secret for a while. And when I mentioned "Bezanija," this is a part of Belgrade which is in the new part of the town of Belgrade, and this is where my wife's sister resided with her husband, and they took them and 15 or 16 more people and they stayed there for several days, up to the moment when all these people could find better accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were your wife and sons given the status of refugees in the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My brother-in-law said that that would be best for them to report to the Red Cross and to take refugee IDs so as to avoid problems. Already after two days they reported to the Red Cross as residents in Bezanija and they obtained refugee IDs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How old was Mirel at that time, your son Mirel?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My son Mirel was 17 at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was he a student at that time? Did he attend a secondary school?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was in the fourth grade of the secondary school for economics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did he continue his education in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He completed the fourth grade of the school of economics in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In what year was that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in 1992, when he started, and completed it in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Why did your stepson, Denis, also decide to become a refugee in Serbia? Why did he go as well?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Denis left because that was my wife's wish. And to be honest, it was also my own wish. I did not want to separate members of my family and listening to these other Serbs talking about balijas and Turks I was aware of the fact that my stepson's parents were both Muslims and I could only assume that if things went pear-shaped what his lot would be. That's why I decided that he should leave together with my wife, despite the fact that he was not a minor at the time and he was a member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: A few days later, did something happen to the commander of the 4th Detachment, Mr. Radovan Antic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How did you learn about that, about something having happened to him?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from him personally. This happened to him a few days after the problem that I had with the gentlemen called Crni, Debeli, and Vuk in the public security station. The problem that Mr. Antic had arose in the department store, where Mr. Stevan Todorovic moved, together with some of his security service, because this was a much more secure building than the public security station, which was on the banks of the River Sava.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did Mr. Antic tell you? What had happened to him in the public security station?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he had been called to come to the public security station which was in the department store. Apparently Mr. Antic was to meet his commander there. Actually, that he was required to go there by Mr. Stevan Todorovic, the chief of the public security station, and some other people. He went there immediately without ever giving a second thought to what could happen to him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told us -- he was very shattered when he was telling us his story. When he arrived there in the office of the commander, there was Mr. Lugar, there was also Mr. Stevan Todorovic, and again Lugar started talking to Radovan Antic about the announcement. Again -- again a question was raised as to why the army, that is, the Communists did that, and he was asked "How long did you Communists intend to behave like that?" These were the words that were addressed to Mr. Antic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Antic physically mistreated?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When Mr. Antic said he had nothing to do with it, because Mr. Antic speaks in a way similar to the way I speak, and when he said to them that what they were saying had nothing to do with the truth, he was knocked out by Lugar and thrown under the table, where Mr. Todorovic was, and Mr. Todorovic and Mr. Radovan Antic come from the same village, which is called Batkusa, and they were next-door neighbours there, because Todorovic comes from Donja Slatina and Mr. Antic comes from Batkusa, so that they were neighbours and they knew each other from before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, I would like to -- to ask the witness through which channels does he have this kind of information? Because I -- I think that he wasn't present when -- when these things happened. So could you please ask him, or I can ask him. How do you know about what was happening in the department store about which you are telling us now? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you have heard His Honour's question. How do you know what happened?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very beginning, when you asked me about this, I said that I heard all this from Commander Antic, so that the details of what happened to him there is what I heard directly from Commander Antic, who told us about it when the whole episode was over, and when he was brought back from Obudovac on the following day, where they locked him up after he came to the command. Commander Antic told us in the command of the 4th Detachment how he was knocked out and so on and so forth. I hope this is clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: This is clear enough, and it means that you have no direct knowledge about what happened. It's a kind of hearsay. Somebody told you; Mr. Antic. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are correct, Your Honour. What I said is what I heard from Commander Antic personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, in your reply just now you said that Mr. Antic had been locked up somewhere. Where had he been locked up?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told us that after this they put him in a car and took him through Gornja Slatina in the direction of Obudovac. There they put him not far from where there's a soccer field in Obudovac and where this special purpose unit was accommodated, and throughout that night, until the following morning when he was released, he was locked up in a toilet which was in a shed outside and he had to actually crouch over the toilet the whole night. That's what he told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who let him go? Who released him from there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he was released by one of the leaders of the special purpose unit. He thinks it was Debeli, as far as I can remember, but I'm not sure. All I know is that on the following morning he was told that he was free to leave and he came to Samac and he told us this whole story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry, excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. Mr. Zaric, did you see any visible injuries on the person of Commander Antic resulting from this experience he had in the department store?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Antic had a big blue bruise under his eye on his head, on his cheek, for at least a week or maybe ten days. He told us that Lugar had hit him. And in addition to all his other characteristics, Lugar was an active boxer for the Radnicki club from Klagurevac [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion did Mr. Antic say how he felt? Did he tell you what his experience was?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very difficult for him. In view of what I had gone through, all I can say is that his experience was even worse than mine. I can't say that he's a more timid man than I am, but he told us in the command that he had been humiliated so badly, and he was the commander of a detachment, that if this happened again he would no longer feel able to lead a unit like ours [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We have one small problem in the transcript. What Mr. Zaric has just said, on page 31, line 15, that after this has happened, not if this happens again. This is not what Mr. Zaric said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe he can repeat what he said slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, what did Mr. Antic say after all these events? Can you please speak slowly so that the interpreters can keep up with you.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that because of what he had gone through and the humiliation, he was no longer able to lead the unit at whose head he was, that he had no strength left psychologically after this humiliating experience. That's what he said in the command where I was and Deputy Jovo Savic and some other people whose names I can't remember at the moment. But he was quite clear about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. And what steps were taken after what Mr. Antic said? Did you inform your superior command of this?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The command of the 17th Tactical Group was informed immediately, and on the same day in the afternoon Mr. Radovan Antic, Mr. Jovo Savic, and I went to Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to talk to the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, to Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and Mr. Makso Simeunovic was also there, as was the chief of staff, Major Brajkovic and maybe some other men, but I am certain that those three were present when we arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did Commander Nikolic say to Mr. Antic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mr. Antic told him his story, the one I have already mentioned here, and told them what his position was, Mr. Nikolic tried to convince Commander Antic to stay on as the commander and not to be discouraged. He mentioned what had happened to me. I mean, what had happened a few days previously. And he said, "You see? Simo has managed to gather the strength to continue. We mustn't give way before them. We mustn't show them we are cowards." What he said was all to this effect, and this was Nikolic speaking to Commander Antic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: After this, did Mr. Antic stay on as the commander of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have to say that in spite of the words spoken by Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic, in spite of the fact that I believed that Mr. Antic would muster the courage and stay with us in the command of the 4th Detachment, he remained determined. He said he could not go on, and he begged the commander to find some other solution and to assign him to some other duty within the 4th Detachment or somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Commander Antic issue any orders on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have to say that there was no time to waste, so that Commander Nikolic said, "Mr. Savic, from this moment you will take over the duty of commander of the 4th Detachment and Radovan, what would you like to do? How can we solve your problem?" Radovan said he would like to do some engineering work, if that could be of any use. And on that occasion, that was agreed and the personnel officer in the command immediately typed out a decision, and Captain Jovo Savic was then appointed commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did Radovan Antic do in the 4th Detachment after this?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He carried out tasks connected with engineering as a special field, and this was on the ground in the area of responsibility of the 4th Detachment, and actually this was building dugouts on the dykes or embankments that I have already mentioned during my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, can you tell us something about the situation in the town of Bosanski Samac in those first days of the war? Was there any shelling? What was the situation like in general?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We cannot say anything good about those days in any area. The war had started, and the first victims fell. On the 18th we had a man killed and one seriously wounded and an infantry attack by the HVO from Prud over the bridge on the River Bosna leading to my native village of Trnjak and the village of Prud which is in the direction of Odzak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember when this infantry attack took place by the forces of the HVO over the bridge on the River Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the morning hours of the 18th, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were there any casualties?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of our men was killed, and one was wounded. The wounded man, however, was wounded in the afternoon of the 17th, while the one who was killed was killed on the 18th of April in the morning and he was killed by a shell from a recoilless gun which had been fired from the direction of Prud. In this infantry attack, when the HVO forces started, our forces returned fire on the defence line facing Prud and then several enemy soldiers were killed on the side of the bridge that is nearer to the village of Prud.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, you mentioned some arrests of citizens of Bosanski Samac. Who did you inform of these arrests?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the very first moment, as soon as I learned of any problems, I immediately informed Mr. Makso Simeunovic. I wrote official notes, and on many occasions I also informed him orally whenever I had an opportunity to do so. From the very first day, everything that happened and everything that I was able to observe as a negative phenomenon I immediately informed Mr. Makso Simeunovic in a very professional manner and a very proper manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you also inform Commander Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I was in the command, and if the commander was there, yes, then I always told him. Of course, I informed Commander Nikolic in general of any large-scale problems, and I informed my superior officer in detail about many other matters that I didn't want to burden Commander Nikolic with, in view of his responsibilities as the commander of the 17th Tactical Group. And I did this as an intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Simeunovic and Mr. Nikolic order anything for you to do regarding the gathering of information of significance for the military situation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did they order you to do?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 20th, I received an order - this is the 20th of April - I received an order from Commander Nikolic and from Mr. Makso Simeunovic that I needed to go to carry out a number of informative talks at the public security station with certain people aimed at checking illegal weapons or illegal arming in the area of Bosanski Samac and the possible inclusion of some -- and the possible participation of some JNA personnel in such arming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, a moment ago my learned friend Mr. Pisarevic at page 20, line 16 said, "Thank you, Mr. Zaric. You mentioned some arrests of citizens of Bosanski Samac. Who did you inform of these arrests?" The Prosecution just requires clarification of what arrests we're talk of and when. In our submission it's more appropriately dealt with in examination-in-chief, these sorts of things, than cross-examination, as it appears to be important for Mr. Zaric's defence. So I ask that this be fleshed out a bit. And of course the negative phenomenon that he referred to a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure Mr. Pisarevic will deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What information did you have, Mr. Zaric, about who was arrested in the town of Samac in that period, on the 17th, the 18th, and the 19th? Who did the arresting and under whose authority were the arrested persons placed and where were they detained?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the part of my testimony -- before, I've already talked about some of these things. The information about the first arrests was something that I already had on the 17th and the 18th, and this is why I received the order to go and for the members of the 4th Detachment, who were already there, to be released. I also said that on that occasion I saw the logbook with the officer on duty, Ilija Lukovic, which I went through to see which members of the 4th Detachment were there and that I saw in that book the names of 30 or 40 people who had already been arrested, all the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You saw their names in that book?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't see their faces?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see their faces. I saw the names of the persons in the logbook that was in the possession of the officer on duty, Ilija Lukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: These 30 or 40 people were not members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were about six or seven members of the 4th Detachment amongst these people. All the other arrested persons were persons of Croat or Muslim ethnicity. Dragan Markovic was also the one-and-only Serb, if I can put it like that, who was on that list and who was detained at the time, according to what was written in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And when did you receive this order from Mr. Simeunovic and Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that it's a problem for me, in view of what I had already experienced at the public security station. So how could I go there and how should I behave once I go there? But Commander Nikolic actually told me that he informed Mr. Stevan Todorovic, the chief of the public security station, that there was a need for a part of the interviews to be carried out there with people who were detained there and that Simo Zaric would come to conduct a part of those interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do at the police station when you went there? Where did you go? What did you actually do while you were at the police station?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got to the police station for the first time, this was sometime on the 20th of April in the morning, I reported to Mr. Todorovic out of a certain kind of discipline because Mr. Nikolic told me that he had already been informed and that I should just go there and tell him that this was something that has already been agreed. I found Stevan Todorovic in an office with a number of members of the multi-coloureds, and these premises at the Secretariat for Internal Affairs, which I could see immediately after that because he sent me there and told me to go there and report to Milos Savic, the chief of the crime division, because Milos Savic was performing the duties of the chief of the crime division at the public security station. The image that I saw at the public security station at the time was really horrendous. Papers were strewn all over the place. The cashiers' boxes were opened in all kinds of ways. You could see that this was a classic break-in. As soon as I talked to Milos and Mr. Vlado Sarkanovic, I got the information - they were actually carrying out the duties in the crime department - I got the information that this had already disappeared, all of it had disappeared. There were no personal identity cards, no travel documents, no driver's licences, no stamps. There were no specific forms which were used by the citizens. So this entire team of the new special forces that arrived apparently knew what was the first thing that they needed to do once you come to the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, when you said just now that there were no personal identity cards, there were no forms, what did you mean? Did you mean the forms for the identity cards?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I thought I meant, the forms necessary to apply for ID cards, for driver's licences, for vehicle registration documents, for travel documents, all of these forms which were kept in the general and administrative affairs department in any public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And did you go to see the chief of the crime division, Mr. Milos Savic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went to see Mr. Milos, whom I knew from before. Before the war, he was performing the functions of the chief of the crime division, and he worked in that department when Dragan Lukac was appointed as acting chief of the public security station. I also knew Mr. Sarkanovic from the period when I worked at the service and after that also. I said that I -- I told them that this was the task that was given to me and that I would like, based on the conducted interviews that they already had and based on the information that they have, I said that I needed to get some information that was most important for me, and what was most important to me was the illegal arming and whether some officers of the JNA participated in this by way of some warehouses, depots, and so on. That was my main intention. And I told this to Mr. Sarkanovic and Mr. Milos.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Savic and Mr. Sarkanovic give you access to the statements that were already taken?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. There were a few, not many I must say, because I got there on the 20th, so this was still at the stage of -- at the early stage. So they had some statements there. They also had some material which they showed to me. This was the material that was found in the office and that related to the defence plan of the Party for Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: We will discuss this a little later. Did you conduct an informative talk on that day with Mr. Sulejman Tihic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the intention, but that day Vlado Sarkanovic told me that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't think the wording of this was translated well. It was translated literally, but the meaning of Mr. Zaric's words, it's not "that was the intention." It just happened that way. This is the correct translation. I mean, literally this is what Mr. Zaric says, but the meaning is -- is that it just happened that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Perhaps in -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I was just about to say that the -- he can give us the answer again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But the question is a little bit ambiguous in my respectful submission. He says, "Did you conduct an informative talk." I'm not quite sure what an informative talk is. Does that mean interview?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. I think we will leave it that way. Let's just see what the answer will be. They use different terms. But what is important is they did discuss something with Mr. Sulejman Tihic. I'm sure, Mr. Zaric, you heard what Mr. Lazarevic was trying to say. Maybe you can go -- you can just give us your answer again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, could you please repeat again what happened and how it happened so that Mr. Tihic happened to be at the crime division.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the occasion of this interview -- of this talk that I had with Mr. Sarkanovic and Mr. Savic, Mr. Vlado Sarkanovic told me that he was about to conduct an interview with Mr. Sulejman Tihic and that he was expecting at any moment for one of the guards to bring Mr. Tihic in for an interview, for an informative talk. I'm saying "an informative talk," but you can also take that to mean an official interview. This is something that we use the term "informative talk" for.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And after you found this out from Mr. Vlado Sarkanovic, was Mr. Tihic brought to this office where you were with Sarkanovic and Savic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after a few minutes Mr. Sulejman Tihic was brought to this room. I said hello to Mr. Tihic. Mr. Sarkanovic and Mr. Savic did the same thing, and we sat down in one of the common rooms, all four of us, and talked for a few minutes, all of us together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On page 41, line 8, it is translated, "I said hello to Mr. Tihic." What Mr. Zaric said was, "I greeted Mr. Tihic in proper and human way." These are the words that he said. He didn't say "hello."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It doesn't make much difference, anyway. Let's proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What was the relationship between you and Mr. Tihic like before the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: After that, did you continue to talk to Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had some coffee together there. Of course, Mr. Tihic was quite upset. His state of mind was disturbed, and this was evident, you could notice that. And this was a conversation with people that he knew, so he wasn't expecting for anything bad to happen, so maybe at this point this was something that he felt was good. So after we drank the coffee, I said that it would be best if Mr. Tihic and I conducted our interview, and I said since -- we called Sulejman Tihic "Mane" in Samac. I asked him, Mane, is there a problem for the two of us to have an interview? To which Mr. Tihic replied there would be no problem at all and that he would actually prefer to have this interview with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did you and Mr. Tihic talk about?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Tihic, once we were left alone in one of those rooms, there are three rooms like that which belong to the criminal investigations department, and Mr. Tihic and I were in one of those rooms, while Mr. Sarkanovic and Milos went to the other two rooms and they were conducting interviews there with other people. First we talked about the fact generally before we even got to any official relations. We talked about how and in what way Mr. Tihic was arrested. He told me that he was at the Radio Samac building and that he was reading a text that was written for him and that he had read this text out in the presence of Mr. Vaso Antic, as the editor-in-chief of Radio Samac. I told Mr. Tihic that I had the opportunity to hear this conversation only once, or his address to the citizens of Samac, but that I had heard that this announcement of his would broadcast on Radio Samac several times because someone probably ordered that this appeal of his and his voice be heard several times throughout the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What else did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then we came to the topic of illegal arming and we talked about the issue of documents which I received from Mr. Milos Savic relating to the military or war plan of the Party for Democratic Action. This was the main topic of our interview throughout that whole day. This was on the 20th. That's the day that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: While you were talking with Mr. Tihic, did somebody call you from any of the other offices?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point, while Mr. Tihic and I were talking, a special came knocking on the door. I heard other people calling him Laki [Realtime transcript read in error "Lucky"]. He opened the door and told me, "Boss, you are needed by Mr. Todorovic, Crni, and another man in the office there. They need you just briefly."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You've used the word "boss." What did he mean when he called you boss? How did you understand that word, when he addressed you as boss? Were you indeed his boss, or is that a popular way of address?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a boss of his, but this lad, this special, addressed people like that all the time. That was his standard behaviour. He would use certain words. He referred to himself as somebody who has the authority, but he was a beast down underneath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. Page 43, line 7, concerning this gentleman who came into the room, he's listed here as being called Lucky, L-u-c-k-y. It's Laki, isn't it? Can we get a clarification of the actual name and maybe how it's spelled?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: L-a-k-i.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Laki, was that his name or his nickname?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was his nickname, and all the time they used nicknames rather than names. That's how he was introduced to everybody, and he always referred to himself as Laki.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you ever learn his real name?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on I learned that his family name was Lazarevic. I didn't know his first name. I never knew his first name, but his last name was Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did you go there? Where did you go to, which office?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The office where I was talking with Mr. Sulejman Tihic was on the upper floor, at the end of the corridor, and the gentlemen who wanted to see me were in the office which was at the far end of that same corridor. I said to Mane, "You can give a second thought to all the things that we have discussed so far [as interpreted]. I'll be back very soon." I came to this office at the far end of the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
