utterances.text: One second. The meaning of what Mr. Zaric said was a different one. Here on the transcript on page 44, line 10, here it says "I said to Mane `you can give a second thought to all the things that we have discussed so far'", and what Mr. Zaric said was, "Mane, you can put on paper if you remember something more."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's a very different --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's a very different meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pisarevic, you can go over that again so that we can get it from Mr. Zaric himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, as you were leaving the office where you were with Mr. Tihic, what exactly did you tell him and what did you mean by using this word, to do a thesis? When translated from the Serbian, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant to put on paper certain things that we would later discuss. I used the word "thesis." What I meant was to make some bullet points of the things that we would discuss. I did not tell him to give it a second thought but to put certain things on paper that we would later on discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to that other office, and that's where I found Mr. Todorovic, Mr. Dragan Djordjevic, Crni. At that time I knew him only by his nickname Crni, but now I know his full name. I hope it won't be a problem if I mention his full name, although I didn't know him at that -- know it at that time. And there was also another gentleman, in civilian clothes. They referred to him as "Major." I know that his first name was Nikola. They referred to him as Major Nikola, and they introduced him to me as somebody from the air force and the anti-aircraft defence of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Mr. Zaric, what did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Todorovic asked me what did the comrade tell you? When he used the word "comrade," in our former system that was a very common word, a very popular word among the people and among the politicians [as interpreted]. It was associated with the League of Communists. Up to the first multi-party elections, Mr. Tihic was --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I have to intervene. Mr. Zaric should really speak slower. On page 45, he didn't say that the word comrade was a very popular word among the politicians but among members of the Communist Party. This is how they addressed each other. Members of the Communist Party addressed each other as "comrade." It has nothing to do with politicians or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to speak as slowly as possible, and I don't seem to be able to do that. There are still mistakes. I will really try to speak as slowly as possible. When he said, "How's our comrade," I tried to explain why he used the word "comrade." At that moment it was a derogatory word. When he said that, he knew that up to the multi-party elections Mr. Tihic and I were members of the League of Communists. And then I said, "There are no problems." I replied to Mr. Todorovic's questions in a very official way. I had already been used to his way of communication and to his way of provocations. This gentleman, to whom they referred as Major, and whom I saw for the first time, the gentleman whose first name was Nikola and for whom they told me that he is a member of the air force and the anti-aircraft defence of the Army of Yugoslavia, he only told me this: "Mr. Zaric, how is the interview with Mr. Tihic getting on?" I replied, "We are having a very correct interview, a very correct conversation, and personally I believe that Mr. Tihic is a very correct person and that I will be in the position to take his statement within a few hours and that by the end of the day this statement should be completed." This was more or less everything that I heard or said in that room. It only took a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you returned to the office where Mr. Tihic had remained sitting, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw something really ugly and absolutely incredible. Mr. Tihic was sitting at a desk. He had paper handkerchiefs in his hand and he was covered with blood. The blood was dripping on the piece of paper in front of him. He had written down something on that paper. When I entered the office and when I saw him in that wretched state, in sheer disbelief I asked him, "Mane, what happened?"

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did Mr. Tihic tell you? What happened?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic told me, "The gentleman who had come to invite you to that meeting, he came back. He beat me up." Mr. Tihic had been beaten on his face. His nose was broken. He was bloody all over. There was blood on his shirt, on the front part of his shirt. He was in a very shattered condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you do next, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I turned around very fast, and I went back to the other office, the office where Mr. Todorovic, Major Nikola from the air force and the anti-aircraft defence of Yugoslavia, and Mr. Crni were, the gentlemen that I had spoken with only a minute before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you tell them?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I addressed Mr. Todorovic and told him, "What kind of a scenario are you trying to stage for me? While I've been talking to you here, and when I got back I found Mr. Tihic covered in blood. Are you trying to set me up? Are you trying to put me in an awkward position by doing that? What are you trying to do?"

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did somebody reply to that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Crni replied and said, "You don't have to feel very sorry for balijas, do you?" Mr. Nikola from the air force and the anti-aircraft defence of Yugoslavia started acting out, I would say. He said, "This really doesn't make sense. Why don't you let the man do his job. Let bygones be bygones." I said to these gentlemen, "I will not allow this kind of treatment. If I talk to people, these people will not be beaten up." And I also told them that "I would immediately inform Mr. Nikolic and my security officer and I will no longer perform this job if such scenes will be a common occurrence from now on."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned to the office and I took Mr. Tihic to the toilet. He washed his face there. He freshened up a bit, and he came to his senses just a little. And then we returned to the office. I apologised most sincerely to Mr. Tihic for what he had been through, and I asked him, "Mane, don't you think it would be good for us to interrupt this interview and continue it tomorrow?" I said that because I saw what state he was in. Mr. Tihic answered me, "Please don't go. They will kill me here. I can continue talking to you -- I prefer talking to you rather than to go through something similar again."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you continue talking to him?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Very often during that day Vlado Sarkanovic would drop by in that office where I was conducting an interview with Mr. Tihic. At one point he saw what had happened, and I also told him in very brief outlines what had happened. Then I asked Vlado to talk to a lady called Andja. She was a typist, and she would type out statements after interviews. I believe that her name was Andja Pupcevic or maybe Petkovic. I'm not sure. She was a typist in the crime department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric is referring or mentioning the word "interview" with Mr. Tihic. What did you interview him about and what is the meaning of the word "interview"? Could you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can tell you that. I talked with Mr. Tihic about the illegal arming of paramilitary formations. During that interview I used that term to talk about the things which the party of democratic action was doing before the outbreak of conflicts. I also talked about Mr. Tihic about the drafting of the war plan of the party of democratic action and how they established their paramilitary units. We also discussed about his best knowledge that he had about the quantity of illegal arms in the possession of Muslim units. And I also wanted to know how much he knew about that, which important meetings he attended, the meetings at which some important things were discussed, including the important meeting that took place in Prud on the 21st of March, 1992. Those were, generally speaking, our major topics. Finally, I took an official statement from Mr. Tihic, and this was one of the exhibits during the trial, I believe. I am not sure, but I believe that it has been presented here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: If I may continue. Who were you representing while asking and interviewing Mr. Tihic? How did you conceive your role at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that under orders from my commander, the command of the 17th Tactical Group, and my superior officer for security, Mr. Makso Simeunovic, I was given the task of carrying out a certain number of interviews in the public security station with a view to obtaining information connected to illegal arming and the organisation of paramilitary formations by the parties of the HDZ and the SDA and certain activities of illegal arming of people through depots of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you so much. When you are talking about illegal arming, this is a very ambiguous concept. When is arming illegal, as to your understanding, and when is it legal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view, the way I saw and understood the problem is as follows: At that time, the JNA --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Please be brief. And don't, so to say -- just answer my question, and don't go back into history and whatever. Just answer me what is legal arming and what is illegal arming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything that the national parties in the pre-war period did to arm their members, which was not connected to the official defence component, the JNA, all this, in my view, was illegal arming, because I am deeply convinced that political parties should act by political means, rather than arming their members with weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, you mean that -- let's say, put it straight. Muslims, Croats, and Serbs who were possessing weapons, they were all illegal, except for the possession of weapons handed over to them by the 4th Detachment? Is that what you are trying to tell me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, when drawing up this statement, did you enter correctly what Mr. Tihic told you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everything that Mr. Tihic found it necessary to say in answer to the questions I put to him, all this I entered into the statement, the statement was typed out, Mr. Tihic read it, he signed it in his own hand, and I think this was done in the most professional manner possible and quite properly, as far as the taking of statements goes. Although, I do understand the position in which Mr. Tihic found himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, while you were drawing up the statement, did you have any knowledge about the activities of Mr. Tihic which were not entered into the statement?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have certain information, and I have to say quite honestly that I didn't want to enter this information into the statement in order not to make his position more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When did you finish your interview with Tihic and the drawing up of the statement?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement was taken in the late afternoon. I might say quite late in the afternoon. It could have been 1600 hours, perhaps. It was springtime and it was starting to get dark. We stayed there because Tihic wanted me to stay with him for as long as possible in order to stop something happening to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: After this, did you receive any sort of request from Mr. Tihic? Did he ask you if he could speak to someone on the phone?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have to say that during the day, and when we first sat down to have some coffee, Mr. Milos Savic, as the chief of the criminal service, Mr. Vlado Sarkanovic, and I, he asked if there was any possibility for him to be released -- to be released and not to be in the situation he was in. Mr. Milos replied that this did not depend on him but that they must take a statement and then Mr. Todorovic would decide. He was the only one who could say who was to be released and who could not be released. When Mr. Tihic and I completed the statement, he said, "Simo, is it at all possible - it's getting dark - for me not to stay in prison? Is there any chance for me to get out of here?" And I said to him, "I know Stevo is the one who's going to decide about this. The only thing I can do is try to talk to Mr. Blagoje Simic, to see if he can have any influence, because until yesterday you were both politicians, working shoulder to shoulder. You were in the parliament of Samac together. So why couldn't the two of you have a chat about this?"

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was very pleased, and he asked whether he could talk to Mr. Blagoje Simic. So I called up Mr. Simic from the office where I was sitting with Mr. Tihic, and this was in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did you and Mr. Blagoje Simic talk about?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I let Mr. Simic know that I had completed an interview with Mr. Tihic, acting under orders from my superior command, and that I had completed the task and that now the fate of Mr. Tihic was to be decided, so I asked Blagoje if there was any way that something could be done and I told him that Mr. Tihic was sitting right next to me and listening to our conversation. I said, "He would like to talk to you directly. What I have talked about with Mr. Tihic is quite enough. It's possible to talk to this man and to release him." That's what I said to Mr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did Mr. Sulejman Tihic talk to Mr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they did talk. Because after what I said, Blagoje said to me, "Very well. Let me speak to Tihic." And I passed the receiver to Mr. Tihic, and then Mr. Tihic and Mr. Blagoje continued the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what they talked about?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the words -- or some of the words that Mr. Tihic spoke at the time. Of course, I didn't know what Mr. Blagoje was answering at the other end, but I could draw some conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did Mr. Tihic say to Mr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic said something like this: "Blagoje, I know the situation is out of control. I had no idea what all these things would lead to." That's how I understood what he said. He said, "Please, I have addressed the citizens of Samac, and I think this was useful. It will be far more useful if I am released, if I can go among those people and be active among them, because I have some authority among the Muslims. Please do something to have me released from this prison." This, to the best of my recollection, is the purpose of what Mr. Tihic said, as I can best paraphrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Shall we take our break?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll continue our proceedings at 18.05.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we'll proceed, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, Mr. Zaric, we talked about how Mr. Tihic and Mr. Blagoje Simic spoke on the phone. When they finished their conversation, did you again speak on the telephone with Mr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did you talk about then?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Blagoje asked me, "What do you suggest?" And I said to Mr. Blagoje, "I suggest that Stevan Todorovic, Mr. Tihic, and I come to see you and that we discuss this and then that we release the man, because he has made a statement, we have his announcement, I think that Sulejman Tihic is needed more among the people than in prison at this moment." Mr. Blagoje Simic replied to this, saying, "Stevo --" meaning Stevan Todorovic, "is Stevo somewhere around? Is he in the station?" I said I had heard that he had been there but I hadn't seen him in the last few hours. Mr. Blagoje then told me to try and check whether Mr. Todorovic was there, whether he was at the station, and that the three of us should go to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the three of us," can you give us the names? What three men were to go to Mr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant Mr. Tihic, Mr. Stevan Todorovic, as the chief of the public security station, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you then finish your conversation with Mr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Blagoje was then in the office, in the agricultural complex. And I said, "As soon as I have a chance --"

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We have -- oh, yes, maybe now it will be corrected. Yes. It's all right now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said to Mr. Blagoje, "As soon as I find Stevo or contact him, I'll do my best to have the three of us come and see you in the office where the Crisis Staff was, together with Mr. Blagoje."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you try to find Stevan Todorovic and did you find him in the end?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did try. I called the duty officer in the public security station and asked him if the chief was there. He said the chief had been in the building a short while before. He wasn't sure where he was exactly. And I said if at all possible that -- I asked him to find him and to bring him to the office where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did Mr. Stevan Todorovic finally show up in the office, and after how much time from the moment you left this message to the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did call about two hours later. In the meantime, I had called the duty officer several times to ask if they had established contact with him, and the answer was that they were looking for him and that they still hadn't found him. After more than two hours, he burst into the office where I was with Mr. Tihic. Mr. Vlado Sarkanovic was with us. Mr. Milos Saric was with us also. And I think Mr. Milos Culapovic was with us in the office as well. I'm not sure if it was him, but I know there were other people there. However, I'm absolutely certain that the two I've mentioned were in the office with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were you with Mr. Tihic throughout these two hours?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, throughout all this time. And we talked. And when Mr. Blagoje said that he would discuss this, I was encouraged and so was Mr. Vlado Sarkanovic, and we transmitted our optimism to Mr. Tihic, thinking that there was a chance that we would come to an agreement and that Mr. Tihic would be released. That's what we talked about among ourselves before Mr. Todorovic entered the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And when Mr. Todorovic finally turned up, what happened and what did he then say to you and to Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, as I learnt very quickly on the following day, had been sleeping in the communications centre during those two hours. The duty officer had told him, but he said, "No one is to find me until I wake up." Of course, the duty officer didn't want to tell me that he was drunk and that he was sleeping it off. I learned this only on the following day, from Mr. Milos and Mr. Vlado. When Mr. Stevan Todorovic turned up in the office, he was very rude. He said, "What do you want?" Those were the first words he spoke. And he turned towards me and the others who were around the table. I told Mr. Todorovic that I had talked to Mr. Blagoje and that we had agreed for Mr. Tihic and Mr. Todorovic and myself to go for a talk with Mr. Blagoje. And then he said as follows: "Is this perhaps something about Tihic being freed?" I said that I wasn't really fully informed about everything because I didn't want to let him know, but I told him that this was something that was agreed upon and if he didn't believe me, he could call Mr. Blagoje and check if it was true that Mr. Blagoje said that we should come and see him at the agricultural cooperative. That's where Mr. Blagoje Simic's office was. Then he turned to face Mr. Tihic. "Balija, there is no freedom for you." I don't know whether this is okay to use the vulgar terms on that occasion, whether it's okay to repeat that in front of the Trial Chamber. I can repeat what he said. I'm not ashamed to say that. But out of consideration for the Trial Chamber and the participants in the proceedings, I would refrain from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can perhaps use some other terms to convey what was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, I don't think it's necessary. He can simply describe whether he used derogatory terms towards Mr. Tihic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. "You Turks in 1389 and 1361 in the First Balkan War and in the Second Balkan War and in the First World War and in the Second World War, you are now in league with the Pope and the Vatican, and for you and people like you there is no freedom. Get out. And I do not want to be bothered about this any more by anyone." He slammed the door so that I didn't even have time to say, "Stevan, wait." I wanted to tell Mr. Stevan Todorovic to stop. I wanted to say this to him again, but there was no opportunity to do that. After these very terrible words that he spoke, he left us simply frozen, and I had the impression that Mr. Tihic was petrified of fear after those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that that evening you did not go with Mr. Tihic and Mr. Todorovic to see Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't go. After Mr. Todorovic left, there was a deathly silence in the office where we remained. We couldn't find any words. We didn't know what to do. And the first person to say anything was Mr. Vlado Sarkanovic. He said, "Mane, don't worry about this now. We will now arrange for him to go into one of those other rooms, in the room -- in the building so that he doesn't have to go to the TO premises." And then he said, "Things are always clearer in the morning than they are at night, so we will make some kind of arrangement." So then very quickly they took Mr. Tihic out of the office, and I only said, "Mane, I did everything I could, but I am not able to do any more than I did and I'm very sorry about that." And this is what I want to say again today openly in front of the Trial Chamber. This is a very clear, simple truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say one more thing: When they took Mr. Tihic out of the room, Sarkanovic and the guard took him. I don't know where they took him. I called Mr. Blagoje Simic and I said, "Mr. Blagoje, Stevo was here. It's not possible to talk to this man. He doesn't accept anything." And then I told Blagoje more or less what he said, and Blagoje then used a proverb of ours to the effect that "you should neither feed a fool nor take them home." This is a saying. And he said, "What can I do now when he's behaving like that?" And I just said, "Blagoje, I really don't know what, but you are the president of the Crisis Staff. He's the chief of police. I am leaving now. And if anything can be done, then you should do it. If not, at least I want you to know that I am informed you about everything." So this was the last comment of Blagoje, when I informed him that Mr. Stevo did not want to go where he was invited to go by Mr. Blagoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This saying, this proverb, "Do not feed a fool nor take them home," what does that mean? Can you just clarify a little bit? What did you conclude from Mr. Simic's words?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This proverb means that it is best to have nothing to do with people like that. However, it seems that it was our fate in Samac to have such a person, and he wasn't the only one. There were several such people. He was a man who was quite characteristic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did he mean Stevan Todorovic when he used that proverb?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he meant him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to see Mr. Tihic again at the Samac police station after a few days?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How did it come about that you saw Mr. Tihic again at the police station in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened perhaps a week, seven days or so later. I was informed that Mr. Tihic wanted to see me. He was asking for me, and that he wanted to have another interview with me. I received this information, that the duty officer called our duty officer at the command and that he was asking for me. I was out on the field -- in the field at that point. I wasn't at the command of the 4th Detachment. When I reported to the duty officer at the police station to ask why they were asking for me, he said, "Milos Savic told us that Mr. Tihic would like to talk to you. Do you have any time to come to the public security station in Samac?" And I said yes, I would come very quickly, perhaps within the hour at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did you go to the police station?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I went to the police station. This was perhaps already around noon, according to my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you meet with Mr. Tihic at the police station?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found Mr. Tihic at the police station. He was already sitting down with Mr. Vlado Sarkanovic and Mr. Milos Savic in the office when I came.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And these are the offices used by the criminal investigations department?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those are the three offices that that department was using, except on this occasion we were in a sort of room that was in the middle, that had a good view of the TO and the yard -- of the TO building and the yard, and the view from there was much better than during a previous conversation in another room that was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And when you met Mr. Tihic, what did you talk about? What did Mr. Tihic tell you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic told me that he felt it was necessary for him to talk to me again, believing still that I would be able to help to resolve his situation and that he is released from jail perhaps. He told me how he spent the night before, how difficult it was and how they threatened him, that some members of the Sareni were going to hang him, and he said that it was important to him for me to come to the station so that he could tell me about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did Mr. Tihic ask you on that occasion to be present there at the police station to protect him?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since he -- he told me that that night, the night before he was beaten, that he was also beaten upstairs and downstairs, that they had used chilli peppers and put them in his mouth, that some Musa [phoen] and this Laki that I had talked about, how they had beaten him and threatened him and again asked him for money, and then they told him that he would be hanged the next day in the square or somewhere else. This is what he more or less told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did you stay at the police station on that day?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked him, "Did you tell this to Mr. Savic and to Vlado?" And he said, "They know all about this, but they are powerless to do anything." And he felt safe enough to tell me the whole story and asked me to spend that day with him, as if I had some new interest or reason to talk to Tihic, because Mr. Savic and Mr. Sarkanovic had interviews with other prisoners. And my presence was supposed to be a pretext so that I would stay with him that day formally, because I didn't really have anything to talk about with Mr. Tihic, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And while you were in the crime investigations department office, did anything happen at the TO headquarters where certain persons were detained?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When Mr. Tihic and I stayed in that middle room, Tihic asked me could he get up and walk around a little bit. The man was probably kept in these poor conditions in these rooms. And I said, "No problem. Feel free to get up and look around and so on." And at one point while he was walking past the window he said to me, "Look, they're just killing Ibela at the TO yard." Ibela is Ibrahim Salkic, called Ibela, and he has already appeared before this Chamber. Then I came up to the window and stood next to Mr. Tihic because the window was painted halfway with white paint, so you couldn't see from the bottom to the middle but you could see from the middle to the top part of the window, so we could see what was going on through that part of the window in the yard of the TO building. A group of men in the camouflage uniforms were using different objects. Some of them had bars; some had batons; some had wooden poles; some were using their fists. They were simply around him and they kept hitting him in turn, and he was howling and jumping up in a horrible way. These moans were just so terrible. Even though Mr. Salkic is a pretty strong man, I am sure that the beatings that he was receiving were pretty strong and the pain was -- they were causing was pretty strong, and I'm sure that the situation was not tolerable or pleasant for either myself or Mr. Tihic either. And I said to Mr. Tihic, "I never thought that anything like this could happen and that members of my people could behave in this manner and that I was powerless to do anything about it." That was the most difficult thing for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And after that beating of Mr. Salkic, which you and Mr. Tihic saw, did anything else happen at the TO headquarters?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was one incident very soon afterwards. I will remember that day. I remember it well. It was the Orthodox Easter. It was the 26th of April, 1992. Suddenly we sensed that a vehicle was stopping suddenly in front of the police station. We could hear the sound of the engine, and then we could hear the screeching of the tyres, as the brakes were applied, so that Mr. Tihic and I just got up by instinct and went up to the window to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did you see when you got to the window?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we got to the window, Mr. Lugar was in that car. He was dressed in a wonderful -- let me say he was wearing wonderful sports equipment. He was wearing a white tracksuit, a white jacket, white sneakers, and he had a white T-shirt. So he was wearing very smart sports gear, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And where did he go when he came out of the car?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His car was parked to the right, towards the Territorial Defence building. But when he got out of the car, he went into the public security station building first.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When Mr. Tihic saw Lugar, did he tell you something? Was he scared?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was scared. And he said, "Simo, I'm sure he is going to kill me. That will be the end of me." That was more or less what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mr. Lugar entered the public security station, I really thought that he would come to us, and I took Tihic to a next-door office. I locked him up there, I took the key, and I returned to the first room, to the first office. Later on, I heard that he hadn't shown any interest in seeing Mr. Tihic, but the two of us were afraid. We were afraid that his arrival was not just an accident, that he had very particular intentions, and that's why I locked Mr. Tihic up in that other room that I have just described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: When this event was occurring, were you armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only thing I had was 7.62-millimetre pistol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: As an officer of my army, why didn't you kill Lugar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you really think I should have done that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I had killed Lugar, then I am sure I wouldn't be sitting here today and my family would have never seen me alive after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: That is no proper explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, don't respond. Just proceed with your evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, when you realised that Mr. Lugar was not coming up, that he was not looking for Mr. Tihic, did you return Mr. Tihic to that first office, to the office where he was previously?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But before I returned him there -- I would like to say something else. When Lugar returned and was somewhere in the middle of that street between the public security station and the Territorial Defence headquarters, he yelled very loud, "Song. Song," in the Ekavian dialect, the way people from Serbia speak. After he uttered that word "song," that could be heard 50 metres around the buildings. All the detainees in the Territorial Defence headquarters started singing pro-Chetnik songs about Draza Mihajlovic, about Topola, and about the guards of General Draza.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. And then you returned Mr. Tihic after that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not immediately. Mr. Lugar asked for the gate of the Territorial Defence headquarters to be opened. Then he went there, and it was only then that I returned Mr. Tihic to the room where I was. And as of that moment on, the two of us observed everything that went on across the road when he entered the courtyard of the Territorial Defence headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: While you were observing, what did you see? What was going on in the Territorial Defence headquarters, the building that is across the road from the public security station?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the detainees were in one room. Lugar gave an order to the guard to open that room. He entered the room, and the song became louder by the minute, because he would ask them to sing louder and then they would start singing louder. So their choir became so loud that one could see them hundreds of metres away from that building. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What happened after that, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then we sat down, and all of a sudden we could hear a shot, one, and another after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you maybe decide where the shots came from?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came from the direction of the Territorial Defence headquarters, the building that Mr. Lugar had gone to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you heard those gunshots, did you do anything?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we heard those gunshots, I called the duty operations officer in the police station. I asked him who was firing, what was going on. The only thing he told me was, "Lugar killed a man."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Having received this information, did you call anybody on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After a certain period of time, through the window we saw a body being pulled out. That's what Mr. Tihic and I saw. The body was pulled out through the door and was put by the door. It was a lifeless body, and Mr. Lugar after that sat in the car with a pistol in his hand. He hit on the gas pedal, the tyre screeched again, and he drove on in an unknown direction towards the eastern part of the town Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who did you call, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once I was sure that the man had been killed, after I received reliable information, very soon after that I learned who that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who was it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Ante Brandic, also known as Dikan, a native of Hasici, a village in the Bosanski Samac municipality. This was a man who was detained in that room. And after the killing, a few minutes later I telephoned Mr. Blagoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did you tell Mr. Blagoje Simic on the phone?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him, "Blagoje, Lugar has just killed a man in the Territorial Defence building." Blagoje responded, "How did that happen?" I said, "I don't know how it happened. I only know that he killed him in front of 50 other men." That's what I told Blagoje, because I assumed that all those men who were in that room were able to see how Dikan was killed, because they were all inside. We couldn't see what was going on, but it was my assumption that there were about 50 people there, and that's why I said that he had killed him in front of 50 other people who all saw that. That's what I said to Mr. Blagoje Simic. And I also told him that this was the last straw, that I would immediately inform my command that people cannot be treated like that and that he, as the president of the Crisis Staff, should do his utmost to prevent any situations like this from happening. This was my exchange with Mr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How did Mr. Blagoje Simic react to those words of yours? What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blagoje told me that he would see what he could do about that, that he had to talk to Stevan Todorovic, the chief, and later on I learnt that at that very moment Mr. Nikolic arrived in the area of Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn that from Mr. Blagoje Simic or from somebody else?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not from Blagoje Simic. Later on I learnt that when I called my command to ask them what was going on. Then I was told that "The commander is with a major, Major Zivanovic, a commander of an armoured unit, and that he said that he would soon be with us." I told him, "Okay, come back soon. I would like to see you as soon as possible."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to Mr. Nikolic on the phone?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you tell him in that telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him, "Commander, a little while ago I was in the public security station, and one of the specials, Lugar, killed a man in front of 50 other people. This is enough. Enough is enough." Since we were already the 26th of April, on the previous days I spoke to him. I informed Makso Simeunovic about tortures and all the other incidents, and Makso Simeunovic reported about that to Commander Nikolic. So Commander Nikolic was up to speed with everything, all the ugly things that were going on in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And then did you ask Commander Nikolic to take some measures?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I asked him to do whatever is possible to help these people out of this inferno for several reasons. For example, now a man was killed without any reason whatsoever. Secondly, I had information available to me according to which people were exposed to all sorts of torture and maltreatment. The building where they were was not secure. If a shell had fallen anywhere near, I don't know how many of them would have survived, and so on and so forth. There are several reasons for us to try and do our utmost to transfer these people to some other more secure place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So what did you agree with Commander Nikolic? What did he say he would do?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said he would have a word with Captain Petrovic. This Captain Petrovic was the security officer [as interpreted] in the 17th Tactical Group and in the garrison of Brcko and he said that he would try and see that Captain Petrovic how could these people under a certain pretext be transferred to the JNA barracks in Brcko so as to be safer, so as to be accommodated in a safer place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There is one word missing here in the transcript. When referring to Captain Petrovic, Mr. Zaric said "this Captain Petrovic was previously the security officer in the 17th Tactical Group," because we already know that Mr. Simeunovic was security officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And after a certain period of time, did Mr. Nikolic inform you about the agreement he had reached with Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he told me that he had had a word with Petrovic, that Petrovic expressed his willingness to carry out this action. I knew that on the 26th of April, which was the Orthodox Easter, this group of specials with Mr. Todorovic and some other men of his from the police were celebrating the Orthodox Easter in a coffee place called Trile, which was some 3 or 4 kilometres away from Samac, and that they all were there in that celebration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Zaric, insist on this action be carried out immediately, during that day or during that night?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I knew that Lugar had come from that coffee bar, did what he did, and returned there, and that's why I said the best thing would be for them to be transferred as soon as possible, while those people were celebrating, because if they were not moved before they return, I didn't know what could happen to these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And finally, did Mr. Nikolic inform you what would be done on that evening?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that Makso Simeunovic would come with a certain number of military policemen, with a necessary number of vehicles, and that these people would be transferred to Brcko. And as for me, that I should make sure that the organisation of their transfer was carried out in the shortest possible time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you received this information from Commander Nikolic, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received this information, and then I returned to the public security station. I found Commander Savo Cancarevic there and Mihajlo Topolovac was also there. I must say that I had a lot of trust in these two people. I told them about the action that was being prepared, and I told them that this action had backing of the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cancarevic and Mr. Topolovac, did they express willingness to participate in that action together with you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They expressed their willingness, and I told them that if they encountered any problems, they could say that this was the order of the army and that then they could talk to his boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean Stevan Todorovic, when you say "his boss"?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Tihic in the police station?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I didn't get involved in finding out who was there, but I said to Mr. Cancarevic and Topolovac to prepare a list as soon as possible because I got information that the car with Mr. Makso Simeunovic would be there very soon. They said they would do it. And when I found out that the action would be carried out, I went to Mr. Tihic, who was in one of the offices upstairs. After our conversation, he remained upstairs all the time. I approached him, and I told him - because this is what I really believed, from the bottom of my heart - I told him, "Mane, I believe you are saved. I had a conversation with Mr. Nikolic and he personally made sure -- will make sure that you are transferred to Brcko, in a safe place. I hope that this will be the end of your troubles." Mane gave me a hug. I gave him a hug. I believe that we even kissed each other sincerely, as two human beings. I was at the time of the opinion, I had a strong belief that him and other people will be saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did Mr. Makso Simeunovic come with the military police of the JNA? Did they arrive in front of that building?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he arrived. He arrived. According to my estimate, it was dark. It may have been around 2200 hours or thereabouts. I met Mr. Makso Simeunovic in front of the offices of the Territorial Defence. They came in two Pinzgauers - that's how we called these vehicles - these Pinzguaers carried the military police armed with automatic rifles and with white belts. There must have been between 15 and 20 people in each of these two vehicles, and there was also another big military vehicle between these two Pinzgauers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you say a military vehicle, you mean a cargo vehicle?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a cargo vehicle with benches on two sides where people can sit. This is the vehicle used for the transportation of troops whenever they go to the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: It was covered with a canvas cloth?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was covered. The top was covered, and the sides were covered with a canvas cloth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where did this vehicle park?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as they arrived, the gate was open. It was a wide gate, wide enough to allow for the passage of a lorry. It reversed into the yard, and the driver parked in the yard not far from the door behind which the detainees from Samac were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, is it time for us to adjourn?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: at 7.00 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 9th day of May, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 25
